title: Idaho Springs dark history exposed by after-dark Ghost Tour
excerpt: At least 14 ethereal enthusiasts gathered outside Tommyknocks Brew Pub in Idaho Springs, ready to embark on The Ghost Tour and learn about the creepy history of our downtown buildings.
content:
At least 14 ethereal enthusiasts gathered outside Tommyknocks Brew Pub in Idaho Springs, ready to embark on The Ghost Tour and learn about the creepy history of our downtown buildings.

The annual tour is set up by the Clear Creek Metropolitan Recreation District. District Sports Coordinator Jessi Steele said she’s spent more than 180 hours researching the historic buildings and some of their spooky pasts.

“The original tour was just based on my fascination with old buildings, finding the history of the buildings,” Steele said.

This year she was apparently upping her game, advertising it would be: “Darker, bolder, and more chilling than ever.”

“Walk the haunted streets, uncover eerie legends, and experience the paranormal like never before.”

Despite her immersive dive into the history of downtown Idaho Springs and the paranormal, Steele encouraged her stories to be taken with “a grain of salt”.

Sit N Chill Ice Cream Shop, 1501 Miner St.

One of the group's first stops was the Sit N Chill Ice Cream shop, a location Steele said has a chilly past.

The building had been used as a furniture store, a bank, but for many years it was the city’s overflow morgue.

In 1970, it would be put to the test in its role as an overflow morgue.

On Oct. 2, 1970, a plane carrying 37 members of the Wichita State University football program and four crew members crashed into the Mount Trelease slope, about 8 miles west of Silver Plume, Colorado; 31 people died.

According to WSU and crash reports, pilot error and the route contributed to the crash.

The pilots chose an unstudied, low-altitude "scenic route" up Clear Creek Valley instead of a standard high-altitude flight path across the mountains.

The aircraft flew too low into the terrain and became trapped in a box canyon near Loveland Pass without enough power to climb to clear the ridge.

The closest location to store the dozens of bodies awaiting autopsy was that morgue in Idaho Springs.

Years later, according to Steele, people reported feeling a cold breeze from nowhere, or a cold hand on your neck, with no one around.

Also, legend says a man, Frank, still inhabits the store; be careful how you talk about Frank, as he has been known to turn lights on and off or violently play with the ceiling fan chains.

Beau Jo's Pizza, 1517 Miner St.

Although Beau Jo’s Pizza is located at 1517 Miner, but there is a door to stairs leading up to the main office at 1519 Miner; according to Steele, there are still some employees who refuse to walk up those stairs.

Staff at the restaurant speak of hearing groaning from under the wooden floorboards, and feelings of someone directly “staring daggers into you,” Steele said.

Then there was the night, not all that long ago, when a female manager was alone in the office counting receipts from the night with the wooden door closed.

A knock on the door got her attention, so she stood to open it; there was no one there.

She returned to her counting when there was another knock on the door; frustrated, she again walked to and opened the door a second time; no one.

Returning to her counting, once again, she was upset at the waste of her time.

However, the third time, there wasn’t a knock; this time someone, or something, was loudly and continually banging on the door.

Apprehensively, the manager opened the door a third time and saw what she would later say looked like a seven-foot shadow of a man staring at her from the end of the hall.

The story is: the figure rushed toward the office, and the manager was able to close the door before it reached her.

The figure was never identified, and the manager and crew determined she was the only one on that floor that night.

Idaho Springs Opera House, 1535 Miner

The building has existed for more than a century and has housed many different shops over the years.

Talk of smelling something burning and hearing the sound of tools in use are common, according to Steele.

There are no tools or fire in place.

Idaho Springs City Hall 1711 Miner St.

The current City Hall building was originally constructed and used as the Grass Valley School.

The building was moved from its original location to 17th and Miner in 1984. It became City Hall in 1986.

Perhaps they are echoes of the school's past, but, according to Steele, patrons and employees can hear frequent writing on a chalkboard, despite the fact that there’s none there.

One employee specifically, Steele said, reported hearing the sound of a young girl giggling from behind an object; the girl wasn’t there.

However, a short time later, what appeared to be a six-year-old girl showed up in the office and asked the employee, ‘Do you want to play hide and seek?’

The small girl left, then walked out of the office only to show up again later that day, asking, “Why didn’t you find me?” 

According to the story, the little girl then disappeared.

Grain of salt?

Members of the tour group listened intently to the stories; a few couples hugged tightly as the tour progressed.

For Jacki Delpiere and her friend Shannon Scane from Michigan, it was their first time in Idaho Springs.

“I think I take it with a grain of salt, but it’s cool to see the old buildings and the history,” Delpiere said.

“All little towns have stories like that, and the history behind the stories is great,” Scane agreed, and both said the tour was well worth it.

For Steele, it was another tour before the end of the season; she said she will go back to researching the town's history and spooky stories for next year’s tour.

“It’s amazing; it’s easily my favorite part of the year,” Steele said.
